summary.text: The proof constructs each witness by taking the binary expansion of a suitable quotient, turning its nonzero bits into distinct parts \(4,8,16,\ldots\); according to \(n\bmod 4\), it then adds none of \(9,18,27\), or respectively one of them, so that the parts sum to \(n\). Every binary part is divisible by \(4\) and each added part by \(9\), hence all are nonsquarefree, while positivity and the total sum place them among the permitted parts and yield a nonempty set of partitions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) denote the number of finite sets \(P\) of positive integers such that
\[
\sum_{x\in P}x=n
\quad\text{and}\quad
x\text{ is not squarefree for every }x\in P.
\]
Using a set rather than a list ensures that the parts are distinct. We prove that for every \(n>23\) there is at least one such set \(P\), which immediately implies \(a(n)>0\).

We begin with an auxiliary construction that will represent any multiple of \(4\) as a sum of distinct nonsquarefree positive integers.

For each nonnegative integer \(m\), define a finite set \(B(m)\) recursively as follows. Put
\[
B(0)=\varnothing.
\]
If \(m>0\), let \(q=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\). If \(m\) is even, set
\[
B(m)=\{2x:x\in B(q)\};
\]
if \(m\) is odd, set
\[
B(m)=\{4\}\cup\{2x:x\in B(q)\}.
\]
This recursion terminates because \(\lfloor m/2\rfloor<m\) whenever \(m>0\). Equivalently, \(B(m)\) consists of the numbers \(4\cdot 2^j\) corresponding to the nonzero binary digits of \(m\). We retain the recursive description because it makes all the needed properties immediate by induction.

We claim that, for every \(m\ge 0\), the following hold:

1. every member of \(B(m)\) is at least \(4\);
2. every member of \(B(m)\) is divisible by \(4\);
3. the sum of all members of \(B(m)\) is \(4m\).

We prove these claims simultaneously by strong induction on \(m\). They are clear for \(m=0\), since \(B(0)\) is empty. Now suppose \(m>0\), put \(q=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\), and assume the claims for \(q\).

First suppose that \(m\) is even, so \(m=2q\). Every member of \(B(m)\) has the form \(2x\) with \(x\in B(q)\). By induction, \(x\ge4\), so \(2x\ge8\), and if \(4\mid x\), then also \(4\mid 2x\). Moreover, multiplication by \(2\) is injective, so it introduces no repetitions, and
\[
\sum_{y\in B(m)}y
 =\sum_{x\in B(q)}2x
 =2\sum_{x\in B(q)}x
 =2(4q)=4(2q)=4m.
\]

Next suppose that \(m\) is odd, so \(m=2q+1\). In this case \(B(m)\) contains \(4\), together with the doubled members of \(B(q)\). The new member \(4\) is positive, at least \(4\), and divisible by \(4\). Every doubled member is at least \(8\) and divisible by \(4\), by the induction hypothesis. In particular, \(4\) is not one of the doubled members, so the union is disjoint. Therefore
\[
\sum_{y\in B(m)}y
 =4+\sum_{x\in B(q)}2x
 =4+2(4q)
 =4+8q
 =4(2q+1)=4m.
\]
This completes the induction and proves all three claims.

The divisibility assertion also shows that every member of every \(B(m)\) is nonsquarefree. Indeed, if \(4\mid x\), then \(2^2\mid x\), so the square of the nonunit integer \(2\) divides \(x\). Thus \(x\) cannot be squarefree. Similarly, every multiple of \(9=3^2\) is nonsquarefree.

Now fix an integer \(n>23\). Thus \(n\ge24\). Write
\[
n=4q+r,
\qquad 0\le r<4,
\]
where \(q=\lfloor n/4\rfloor\) and \(r\in\{0,1,2,3\}\). We construct the desired partition separately in the four possible residue classes.

**Case 1: \(r=0\).** Define
\[
P=B(q).
\]
Then, by the sum property of \(B\),
\[
\sum_{x\in P}x=4q=n.
\]
Every member of \(P\) is positive and divisible by \(4\), hence nonsquarefree. Thus \(P\) is a partition of \(n\) into distinct nonsquarefree parts.

**Case 2: \(r=1\).** Since \(n\ge24\) and \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), in fact \(n\ge25\), so \(q\ge6\); in particular \(q-2\) is a nonnegative integer. Define
\[
P=\{9\}\cup B(q-2).
\]
Every member of \(B(q-2)\) is divisible by \(4\), whereas \(9\) is not divisible by \(4\). Hence \(9\notin B(q-2)\), so this union introduces no repeated part. Its sum is
\[
\sum_{x\in P}x
 =9+4(q-2)
 =9+4q-8
 =4q+1=n.
\]
The part \(9\) is nonsquarefree because \(3^2\mid9\), and all the other parts are positive multiples of \(4\), hence nonsquarefree. Thus \(P\) is an admissible partition.

**Case 3: \(r=2\).** Here \(n\ge26\), so again \(q\ge6\), and therefore \(q-4\ge0\). Define
\[
P=\{18\}\cup B(q-4).
\]
The number \(18\) is not divisible by \(4\), while every member of \(B(q-4)\) is, so \(18\notin B(q-4)\). Consequently all parts in \(P\) are distinct. Also
\[
\sum_{x\in P}x
 =18+4(q-4)
 =18+4q-16
 =4q+2=n.
\]
Since \(9\mid18\), the part \(18\) is nonsquarefree; every member of \(B(q-4)\) is a positive multiple of \(4\), hence is also nonsquarefree. This gives an admissible partition.

**Case 4: \(r=3\).** In this residue class, \(n\ge27\), so \(q\ge6\) and \(q-6\ge0\). Define
\[
P=\{27\}\cup B(q-6).
\]
Again the union has no repetition: \(27\) is not divisible by \(4\), whereas every member of \(B(q-6)\) is divisible by \(4\). Its sum is
\[
\sum_{x\in P}x
 =27+4(q-6)
 =27+4q-24
 =4q+3=n.
\]
The part \(27\) is nonsquarefree because \(9\mid27\), and every other part is a positive multiple of \(4\), hence nonsquarefree. Notice that the boundary value \(n=27\) is handled correctly: then \(q=6\), so \(B(q-6)=B(0)=\varnothing\), and the partition is simply \(\{27\}\).

Thus in every residue class modulo \(4\) we have produced a finite set \(P\) of distinct positive nonsquarefree integers whose sum is \(n\).

For completeness, every part of this set also automatically lies between \(1\) and \(n\), as required if the count is defined by first restricting the possible parts to \(\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\). Positivity was proved above. If \(x\in P\), then all members of \(P\) are nonnegative and
\[
x\le \sum_{y\in P}y=n,
\]
so \(x\le n\).

Therefore the collection counted by \(a(n)\) contains at least the explicitly constructed set \(P\). It is consequently nonempty, and hence its cardinality satisfies
\[
a(n)\ge1>0.
\]
This proves that \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>23\).
